sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
With sinusoids the instantaneous power \(p(t) = v(t)\,i(t)\) wiggles at twice the signal frequency. What matters for heating and energy bills is its **average**. A resistor absorbs average power; an ideal capacitor or inductor absorbs power for half a cycle and returns it the next, so its average is zero.

The **RMS** value is the DC value that would deliver the same average power to a resistor. For a sinusoid it is the peak divided by \(\sqrt2\). Mains "120 V" is an RMS value, about 170 V peak. With phasors, the average power depends on the phase angle between voltage and current, through the **power factor** \(\cos\theta\).
sections.figure_alt: Instantaneous capacitor power alternating equally above and below zero.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ V_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T v^2\,dt}, \qquad V_{rms} = \frac{V_m}{\sqrt2}\ \text{(sinusoid)} \]
\[ P_{avg} = \tfrac12 V_m I_m \cos\theta = V_{rms} I_{rms}\cos\theta, \quad \theta = \angle V - \angle I \]
Complex power: \(S = \tfrac12\,\mathbf{V}\,\mathbf{I}^{*} = P + jQ\).
Resistor: \(P = V_{rms}^2/R\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A load \(Z = 30 + 40j\ \Omega\) is driven by a sinusoid with amplitude \(V_m = 100\ \mathrm{V}\).
\[ |Z| = 50\ \Omega, \quad I_m = \frac{100}{50} = 2\ \mathrm{A}, \quad \theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{40}{30} \approx 53.1^\circ \]
\[ P = \tfrac12 \cdot 100 \cdot 2 \cdot \cos 53.1^\circ = 100 \cdot 0.6 = 60\ \mathrm{W} \]
Check: all real power goes into the resistive part, \(\tfrac12 I_m^2 R = \tfrac12\cdot4\cdot30 = 60\ \mathrm{W}\). ✓

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Mixing peak and RMS values in one formula (an extra or missing factor of 2).
- Using \(|Z|\) in \(V^2/R\); only the resistance absorbs power.
- Forgetting the conjugate in \(S = \tfrac12 VI^*\).
- Assuming the RMS of a non-sinusoidal waveform is also peak\(/\sqrt2\).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: RMS and average power reappear in the op-amp chapter when sizing output swing and in noise analysis, where noise is always quoted as an RMS value and independent sources add in power.
